newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel wants more welfare cuts in '97 budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel wants more welfare cuts in '97 budget.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Thursday that further cuts in social welfare spending must be agreed in the 1997 budget to allow Germany to qualify for European monetary union.

Waigel said the gap to be closed in the federal budget by next week was down to three billion marks ($1.99 billion). One billion marks would have to be cut from transfers to the Federal Labour Office, while the rest would be spread across all ministries.

That would enable Germany to achieve the strict Maastricht Treaty limit on budget deficits of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- one of the main requirements for joining a single European currency in 1999.
"We in the federal government, and I assume that the states will follow, are doing all possible to achieve the deficit criterion of below three percent for 1997 in Germany," Waigel told German radio.
Waigel has set a budget deficit target of 56.5 billion marks -- equivalent to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product.
He said his projections were based on solid ground after German research institutes and European organisations said the economy would grow by between 2.3 and 2.5 percent next year.
But the exact gap which needs to be closed will only become clear when latest tax revenue estimates are released on Friday.
Waigel has overshot borrowing targets this year, mainly due to extra funds needed by the Federal Labour Office to finance unemployment benefits.

The pressure on government finances from the sluggish labour market increased on Thursday with data showing German unemployment rose by 41,000 in October to 4.04 million against September on a seasonally adjusted basis.
Expected economic recovery next year is not expected to ease unemployment, which is at a post-war high.
The Labour Office is funded by unemployment insurance payments, but the Finance Ministry must cover any shortfalls.
Waigel was obliged to make a transfer this year of 14 billion marks, dashing hopes he would meet 1996 budget targets.

"We know that this cannot happen again next year. We cannot afford it," he said. On top of savings of eight billion marks agreed last spring, a further one billion marks would have to come out of the social welfare budget.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition this week found a way out of an internal row over cutting a tax raised to aid east Germany, and can now focus on finalising the budget for submission to parliament's budget committee next week.
A final budget vote is expected in late November.

Coalition sources said that agreement in principle had been reached on cutting the 7.5 percent solidarity tax by two points in 1998. The measure should be finalised in mid-December in talks which will also tackle plans for a major tax reform.

Separately, the Bundestag lower house of parliament held a final reading of Waigel's 1997 tax bill, a compromise measure which has been watered down after a clash with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).

Waigel defended key aspects of the bill, especially the abolition of an assets tax ruled illegal by the constitutional court, and accused the SPD of pursuing the politics of envy by seeking to keep the tax.
"That is no longer a trump card but a red card for investors," Waigel told parliament in an attack on the SPD.

The tax bill was expected to pass through the Bundestag, but will also have to go before the SPD-controlled Bundesrat this month. The Bundesrat may then send the bill back to parliament's mediation committee to iron out a final version.
